blocks.text: **The problem.** A grid of land heights sits between two oceans: the **Pacific** touches its top and left edges, the **Atlantic** its bottom and right edges. Rain flows from a cell to a neighbour (up, down, left or right) that is **no higher** than it, and from any edge cell into the ocean beside it. Return every cell from which water can reach **both** oceans.

blocks.alt: A 5 by 5 grid of heights. The Pacific runs along the top and left edges, the Atlantic along the bottom and right edges. Seven cells are green: from each of them, water can flow downhill into both oceans.

blocks.text: The idea: climb up from the oceans
The direct way is to pour water on every cell and follow it downhill to see which oceans it reaches. That's one search **per cell**, and the searches repeat each other's work over and over.

Start from the border instead, like Surrounded Regions — but now there are two borders. Run water **backwards**: from every Pacific edge cell, walk *uphill*, stepping to any neighbour that is **at least as high**. Every cell this climb reaches can drain into the Pacific, because the path you climbed is a path water can flow down. Do the same from the Atlantic edges. The answer is the cells **both** climbs reached.
1. Brute force: pour water on every cell
For each cell, run a DFS that only steps downhill (or level), and note whether it ever stands on a Pacific edge and on an Atlantic edge.
**Time O((m · n)²), space O(m · n).** Each of the m · n cells may run a search over the whole grid — a nearly flat grid is the worst case, since water can wander almost everywhere from every cell.
One climb from the Pacific edges fills `pacific`, one climb from the Atlantic edges fills `atlantic`. A cell already marked is never climbed again, so each climb visits every cell at most once.

blocks.caption: Climb from the Pacific edges, then from the Atlantic edges; the cells both reach are the answer.

blocks.text: **Time O(m · n), space O(m · n).** Each climb marks a cell at most once and checks its 4 neighbours, and there are only two climbs. The two `reach` grids and the recursion each take O(m · n).

blocks.alt: Pour on every cell: O((m·n)²) time, O(m·n) space. Climb from oceans: O(m·n) time, O(m·n) space.

blocks.text: Reversing the direction of the search turns m · n searches into two. Remember to reverse the **comparison** too: flowing down means `<=`, climbing back up means `>=`.

items: **A single cell** — it touches all four edges, so it reaches both oceans.
**One row or one column** — every cell touches both oceans.
**A flat grid** — water can go anywhere, so every cell is in the answer.
**Equal neighbours** — water flows across level ground, so the climb must use `>=`, not `>`.
**Surrounded Regions** — one border instead of two. Previous lesson.
**Number of Enclaves** — land cells that can't reach any edge: climb from the edges, count the rest.
**Trapping Rain Water II** — water trapped on a 2D height map; also starts from the border, but grows inwards lowest-first with a heap.
